Sturm-Liouville Theory

Purdue University
Course-material provenance

This page was migrated from the CHM 696 course materials developed by Jonathan Hood and Lyudmila Slipchenko. Equations and examples remain under editorial review during the Fall 2026 website migration.

Learning goals¶

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

  • put a second-order eigenvalue ODE into Sturm--Liouville form;

  • identify its coefficient, weight, interval, and boundary conditions;

  • derive orthogonality from the Lagrange boundary form; and

  • recognize the Sturm--Liouville equations for common special functions.

Introduction¶

  • In Fourier series, we used a set of trigonometric functions and demonstrated that they were orthogonal and complete.

  • Sturm-Liouville theory generalizes this concept by describing the relationship between eigenfunctions and ordinary differential equations (ODEs).

  • A regular self-adjoint Sturm--Liouville problem has real eigenvalues and eigenfunctions that are orthogonal with respect to its weight. Under the standard regularity hypotheses, those eigenfunctions are complete in the corresponding weighted L2L^2L2 space.

  • These orthogonal eigenfunctions are powerful tools for analyzing ODEs, such as finding the normal modes of a system, determining time dependence, or intuitively understanding the natural resonances of systems.

Example: second-order ODE¶

  • Consider a second-order linear ordinary differential equation (ODE) of the form:

d2ψ(x)dx2+K2ψ(x)=0.\frac{d^2 \psi(x)}{dx^2} + K^2 \psi(x) = 0.dx2d2ψ(x)​+K2ψ(x)=0.
(1)

  • This equation can be rewritten in operator form as:

Lψ=K2ψ,\mathcal{L} \psi = K^2 \psi,Lψ=K2ψ,
(2)

where L\mathcal{L}L is the differential operator defined by:

L=−d2dx2.\mathcal{L} = -\frac{d^2}{dx^2}.L=−dx2d2​.
(3)

  • This formulation leads to the general eigenvalue problem:

Lψ=λψ,\mathcal{L} \psi = \lambda \psi,Lψ=λψ,
(4)

with boundary conditions ψ(0)=ψ(a)=0\psi(0) = \psi(a) = 0ψ(0)=ψ(a)=0.

  • In this context, ψ\psiψ is the eigenfunction, and λ\lambdaλ is the eigenvalue.

Example: second-order ODE (continued)¶

d2ψ(x)dx2+K2ψ(x)=0\frac{d^2 \psi(x)}{dx^2} + K^2 \psi(x) = 0dx2d2ψ(x)​+K2ψ(x)=0
(5)

  • The boundary conditions require the solution to be represented as a Fourier sine series:

ψn(x)=2asin⁡(nπxa),K=nπa,\psi_n(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{a}} \sin\left( \frac{n \pi x}{a} \right), \quad K = \frac{n \pi}{a},ψn​(x)=a2​​sin(anπx​),K=anπ​,
(6)

where nnn is a positive integer.

  • The normalization ensures that the eigenfunctions are orthonormal over the interval [0,a][0, a][0,a].

Example: second-order ODE (continued)¶

ψn(x)=2asin⁡(nπxa),K=nπa,\psi_n(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{a}} \sin\left( \frac{n \pi x}{a} \right), \quad K = \frac{n \pi}{a},ψn​(x)=a2​​sin(anπx​),K=anπ​,
(7)

  • We can manually verify that these eigenfunctions ψn(x)\psi_n(x)ψn​(x) are orthogonal under the inner product:

∫0aψn(x)∗ψm(x) dx={0if n≠m,1if n=m.\int_0^a \psi_n(x)^* \psi_m(x) \, dx = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } n \neq m, \\ 1 & \text{if } n = m. \end{cases}∫0a​ψn​(x)∗ψm​(x)dx={01​if n=m,if n=m.​
(8)

  • The complex conjugate ψn(x)∗\psi_n(x)^*ψn​(x)∗ is included because the functions could, in general, be complex. The norm of a complex function is given by ∣ψ∣2=ψ∗ψ|\psi|^2 = \psi^* \psi∣ψ∣2=ψ∗ψ.

Dirac notations for inner product¶

  • We now introduce a more general notation for the inner product, which is not yet specific to quantum mechanics. We define:

⟨ψn∣ψm⟩=∫ψn(x)∗ψm(x) dx=δnm,\langle \psi_n | \psi_m \rangle = \int \psi_n(x)^* \psi_m(x) \, dx = \delta_{nm},⟨ψn​∣ψm​⟩=∫ψn​(x)∗ψm​(x)dx=δnm​,
(9)

where the Kronecker delta δnm\delta_{nm}δnm​ is defined as

δnm={1if n=m,0if n≠m.\delta_{nm} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } n = m, \\ 0 & \text{if } n \neq m. \end{cases}δnm​={10​if n=m,if n=m.​
(10)

  • We also introduce the notation for the inner product involving an operator A\mathcal{A}A:

⟨ψn∣A∣ψm⟩=∫ψn(x)∗Aψm(x) dx.\langle \psi_n | \mathcal{A} | \psi_m \rangle = \int \psi_n(x)^* \mathcal{A} \psi_m(x) \, dx.⟨ψn​∣A∣ψm​⟩=∫ψn​(x)∗Aψm​(x)dx.
(11)

This is a matrix element. It is an expectation value only when the same normalized state appears on both sides, ⟨ψ∣A∣ψ⟩\langle\psi|\mathcal A|\psi\rangle⟨ψ∣A∣ψ⟩.

Dirac notations for inner product (continued)¶

  • For example, for the operator L\mathcal{L}L, we have:

∫0aψn(x)∗Lψm(x) dx=λm∫0aψn(x)∗ψm(x) dx,\int_0^a \psi_n(x)^* \mathcal{L} \psi_m(x) \, dx = \lambda_m \int_0^a \psi_n(x)^* \psi_m(x) \, dx,∫0a​ψn​(x)∗Lψm​(x)dx=λm​∫0a​ψn​(x)∗ψm​(x)dx,
(12)

which can be expressed using our new notation as:

⟨ψn∣L∣ψm⟩=λm⟨ψn∣ψm⟩.\langle \psi_n | \mathcal{L} | \psi_m \rangle = \lambda_m \langle \psi_n | \psi_m \rangle.⟨ψn​∣L∣ψm​⟩=λm​⟨ψn​∣ψm​⟩.
(13)

  • Additionally, the operator can act on the first function in the inner product:

⟨Lψn∣ψm⟩=∫(Lψn(x))∗ψm(x) dx.\langle \mathcal{L} \psi_n | \psi_m \rangle = \int (\mathcal{L} \psi_n(x))^* \psi_m(x) \, dx.⟨Lψn​∣ψm​⟩=∫(Lψn​(x))∗ψm​(x)dx.
(14)

  • Similarly,

⟨ψn∣Lψm⟩=⟨ψn∣L∣ψm⟩,\langle \psi_n | \mathcal{L} \psi_m \rangle = \langle \psi_n | \mathcal{L} | \psi_m \rangle,⟨ψn​∣Lψm​⟩=⟨ψn​∣L∣ψm​⟩,
(15)

which highlights the linearity of the inner product operation.

Hermitian operators¶

  • An operator L\mathcal{L}L is called Hermitian (or self-adjoint) if it satisfies:

⟨v∣Lu⟩=⟨Lv∣u⟩\langle v | \mathcal{L} u \rangle = \langle \mathcal{L} v | u \rangle⟨v∣Lu⟩=⟨Lv∣u⟩
(16)

for all functions uuu and vvv in the domain of L\mathcal{L}L, given appropriate boundary conditions.

  • For the operator to be Hermitian, the following condition must hold:

∫abv∗(x)Lu(x) dx=∫ab[Lv(x)]∗u(x) dx\int_a^b v^*(x) \mathcal{L} u(x) \, dx = \int_a^b \left[ \mathcal{L} v(x) \right]^* u(x) \, dx∫ab​v∗(x)Lu(x)dx=∫ab​[Lv(x)]∗u(x)dx
(17)

  • Self-adjointness first implies that every eigenvalue is real. For eigenpairs Lu=λuu\mathcal Lu=\lambda_u uLu=λu​u and Lv=λvv\mathcal Lv=\lambda_v vLv=λv​v,

(λu−λv)∫abv∗(x)u(x) dx=0.(\lambda_u-\lambda_v) \int_a^b v^*(x)u(x)\,dx=0.(λu​−λv​)∫ab​v∗(x)u(x)dx=0.
(18)

  • Thus, the eigenfunctions corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal:

∫abv∗(x)u(x) dx=0ifλu≠λv\int_a^b v^*(x) u(x) \, dx = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad \lambda_u \neq \lambda_v∫ab​v∗(x)u(x)dx=0ifλu​=λv​
(19)

Proof of self-adjointness¶

  • Use the standard Sturm--Liouville expression

Lu=−ddx ⁣[p(x)dudx]+q(x)u,\mathcal{L}u =-\frac{d}{dx}\!\left[p(x)\frac{du}{dx}\right]+q(x)u,Lu=−dxd​[p(x)dxdu​]+q(x)u,
(20)

where ppp and qqq are real and sufficiently regular and p(x)>0p(x)>0p(x)>0 in a regular problem.

  • L\mathcal{L}L is the Sturm--Liouville linear operator.

  • We will now show that this form is self-adjoint. While this does not encompass every second-order ODE, it includes a large and important class of them.

  • To ensure that L\mathcal{L}L is self-adjoint, the operator must satisfy certain conditions, including appropriate behavior at the boundaries. Specifically, the boundary terms arising from integration by parts must vanish.

Proof of self-adjointness (continued)¶

  • Consider the integral:

∫abv∗(x)Lu(x) dx=∫abv∗(x)(−ddx[p(x)dudx]+q(x)u(x))dx\int_a^b v^*(x) \mathcal{L} u(x) \, dx =\int_a^b v^*(x) \left(-\frac{d}{dx}\left[p(x)\frac{du}{dx}\right]+q(x)u(x)\right)dx∫ab​v∗(x)Lu(x)dx=∫ab​v∗(x)(−dxd​[p(x)dxdu​]+q(x)u(x))dx
(21)

  • Integrate by parts:

∫abv∗(x)Lu(x) dx\int_a^b v^*(x) \mathcal{L} u(x) \, dx∫ab​v∗(x)Lu(x)dx
(22)
=−[v∗(x)p(x)u′(x)]ab+∫abv′∗(x)p(x)u′(x) dx+∫abv∗(x)q(x)u(x) dx=-\left[v^*(x)p(x)u'(x)\right]_a^b +\int_a^b v'^*(x)p(x)u'(x)\,dx +\int_a^b v^*(x)q(x)u(x)\,dx=−[v∗(x)p(x)u′(x)]ab​+∫ab​v′∗(x)p(x)u′(x)dx+∫ab​v∗(x)q(x)u(x)dx
(23)

  • Similarly, for ∫ab[Lv(x)]∗u(x) dx\int_a^b \left[ \mathcal{L} v(x) \right]^* u(x) \, dx∫ab​[Lv(x)]∗u(x)dx, we obtain:

∫ab[Lv(x)]∗u(x) dx\int_a^b \left[ \mathcal{L} v(x) \right]^* u(x) \, dx∫ab​[Lv(x)]∗u(x)dx
(24)
=−[p(x)v′∗(x)u(x)]ab+∫abp(x)v′∗(x)u′(x) dx+∫abv∗(x)q(x)u(x) dx=-\left[p(x)v'^*(x)u(x)\right]_a^b +\int_a^b p(x)v'^*(x)u'(x)\,dx +\int_a^b v^*(x)q(x)u(x)\,dx=−[p(x)v′∗(x)u(x)]ab​+∫ab​p(x)v′∗(x)u′(x)dx+∫ab​v∗(x)q(x)u(x)dx
(25)

  • Subtracting the two expressions, the difference involves only the boundary terms

Proof of self-adjointness (continued)¶

  • Subtracting the two expressions, the difference involves only the boundary terms:

∫abv∗(x)Lu(x) dx−∫ab[Lv(x)]∗u(x) dx\int_a^b v^*(x) \mathcal{L} u(x) \, dx - \int_a^b \left[ \mathcal{L} v(x) \right]^* u(x) \, dx∫ab​v∗(x)Lu(x)dx−∫ab​[Lv(x)]∗u(x)dx
(26)
=[p(x)v′∗(x)u(x)−v∗(x)p(x)u′(x)]ab.=\left[p(x)v'^*(x)u(x)-v^*(x)p(x)u'(x)\right]_a^b.=[p(x)v′∗(x)u(x)−v∗(x)p(x)u′(x)]ab​.
(27)

  • For L\mathcal{L}L to be self-adjoint, the boundary terms must vanish:

[v∗(x)p(x)dudx−p(x)dv∗(x)dxu(x)]ab=0.\left[ v^*(x) p(x) \frac{du}{dx} - p(x) \frac{d v^*(x)}{dx} u(x) \right]_a^b = 0.[v∗(x)p(x)dxdu​−p(x)dxdv∗(x)​u(x)]ab​=0.
(28)

  • This condition can be satisfied by appropriate boundary conditions, such as Dirichlet or Neumann conditions.

Proof of self-adjointness (continued)¶

  • For L\mathcal{L}L to be self-adjoint, the boundary terms must vanish:

[v∗(x)p(x)dudx−p(x)dv∗(x)dxu(x)]ab=0.\left[ v^*(x) p(x) \frac{du}{dx} - p(x) \frac{d v^*(x)}{dx} u(x) \right]_a^b = 0.[v∗(x)p(x)dxdu​−p(x)dxdv∗(x)​u(x)]ab​=0.
(29)

  • This condition can be satisfied by appropriate boundary conditions, such as Dirichlet or Neumann conditions. For example:

    • Dirichlet Boundary Conditions: u(a)=u(b)=0u(a) = u(b) = 0u(a)=u(b)=0 and v(a)=v(b)=0v(a) = v(b) = 0v(a)=v(b)=0.

    • Neumann Boundary Conditions: dudx∣x=a=dudx∣x=b=0\frac{du}{dx}\bigg|_{x=a} = \frac{du}{dx}\bigg|_{x=b} = 0dxdu​∣∣​x=a​=dxdu​∣∣​x=b​=0 and dvdx∣x=a=dvdx∣x=b=0\frac{dv}{dx}\bigg|_{x=a} = \frac{dv}{dx}\bigg|_{x=b} = 0dxdv​∣∣​x=a​=dxdv​∣∣​x=b​=0.

    • Mixed Boundary Conditions: A combination of Dirichlet and Neumann conditions at different endpoints.

  • These boundary conditions ensure that the boundary terms vanish, thereby guaranteeing that L\mathcal{L}L is self-adjoint.

Implications of Self-Adjointness¶

The self-adjointness of the operator L\mathcal{L}L has several important consequences:

  • Real Eigenvalues: All eigenvalues λ\lambdaλ of a self-adjoint operator are real.

  • Orthogonal Eigenfunctions: Eigenfunctions corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal under the inner product.

  • Complete Set of Eigenfunctions: The eigenfunctions form a complete basis for the function space under consideration, allowing any sufficiently smooth function to be expressed as a linear combination of the eigenfunctions.

Completeness requires the hypotheses of the relevant spectral theorem; it does not follow from formal symmetry alone.

Sturm–Liouville equations¶

A regular Sturm--Liouville eigenproblem has the form

−ddx ⁣[p(x)y′(x)]+q(x)y(x)=λρ(x)y(x),-\frac{d}{dx}\!\left[p(x)y'(x)\right]+q(x)y(x) =\lambda\rho(x)y(x),−dxd​[p(x)y′(x)]+q(x)y(x)=λρ(x)y(x),
(30)

with real p,q,ρp,q,\rhop,q,ρ, p(x)>0p(x)>0p(x)>0, and ρ(x)>0\rho(x)>0ρ(x)>0 on the interval, together with self-adjoint boundary conditions.

  • This can be written as:

Ly=λρ(x)y,\mathcal{L}y = \lambda \rho(x)y,Ly=λρ(x)y,
(31)

where

Ly≡−ddx ⁣[p(x)y′(x)]+q(x)y(x).\mathcal{L}y \equiv-\frac{d}{dx}\!\left[p(x)y'(x)\right]+q(x)y(x).Ly≡−dxd​[p(x)y′(x)]+q(x)y(x).
(32)

Transforming an equation into Sturm–Liouville form¶

Transforming an equation into Sturm--Liouville form

  • Any second-order differential equation of the form

p(x)d2ydx2+r(x)dydx+q(x)y+λρ(x)y=0p(x)\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + r(x)\frac{dy}{dx} + q(x)y + \lambda \rho(x)y = 0p(x)dx2d2y​+r(x)dxdy​+q(x)y+λρ(x)y=0
(33)

can be converted into Sturm--Liouville form by multiplying through by an integrating factor:

F(x)=exp⁡{∫xr(u)−p′(u)p(u) du}F(x) = \exp \left\{ \int ^x \frac{r(u) - p'(u)}{p(u)}\,du \right\}F(x)=exp{∫xp(u)r(u)−p′(u)​du}
(34)

  • Then the original equation takes the Sturm--Liouville form:

[F(x)p(x)y′]′+F(x)q(x)y+λF(x)ρ(x)y=0[F(x)p(x)y']' + F(x)q(x)y + \lambda F(x)ρ(x)y = 0[F(x)p(x)y′]′+F(x)q(x)y+λF(x)ρ(x)y=0
(35)

Example: converting the ODE into Sturm-Liouville form¶

  • Consider Hermite equation:

y′′−2xy′+2νy=0y'' - 2xy' + 2\nu y = 0y′′−2xy′+2νy=0
(36)

  • Here, p=1p = 1p=1, r=−2xr = -2xr=−2x, q=2νq = 2\nuq=2ν

  • The integrating factor is:

F(x)=exp⁡{∫xr(u)−p′(u)p(u)}=exp⁡{∫x−2udu}=exp⁡(−x2)F(x) = \exp \left\{ \int ^x \frac{r(u) - p'(u)}{p(u)} \right\} = \exp\left\{ \int ^x -2u du \right\} = \exp(-x^2)F(x)=exp{∫xp(u)r(u)−p′(u)​}=exp{∫x−2udu}=exp(−x2)
(37)

  • Thus, the Hermite equation becomes:

e−x2y′′−2xe−x2y′+2νe−x2y=(e−x2y′)′+2νe−x2y=0e^{-x^2}y'' -2xe^{-x^2}y' +2 \nu e^{-x^2} y = (e^{-x^2}y')' +2\nu e^{-x^2}y = 0e−x2y′′−2xe−x2y′+2νe−x2y=(e−x2y′)′+2νe−x2y=0
(38)

  • This equation is in Sturm-Liouville form

(py′)′+q(x)y+λρ(x)y=0(py')' + q(x)y + \lambda \rho(x)y = 0(py′)′+q(x)y+λρ(x)y=0
(39)

with p(x)=e−x2p(x) = e^{-x^2}p(x)=e−x2, q(x)=0q(x) = 0q(x)=0, ρ(x)=e−x2\rho(x)= e^{-x^2}ρ(x)=e−x2, λ=2ν\lambda = 2\nuλ=2ν

The weight function¶

  • The general SL equation:

(py′)′+q(x)y+λρ(x)y=0(py')' + q(x)y + \lambda \rho(x)y = 0(py′)′+q(x)y+λρ(x)y=0
(40)

  • Here, ρ\rhoρ is the weight function.

  • The weight function modifies the inner product defined over the space of functions considered in the problem.

  • The inner product is then defined as:

⟨v,u⟩ρ=∫abv∗(x)u(x)ρ(x) dx\langle v,u\rangle_\rho =\int_a^b v^*(x)u(x)\rho(x)\,dx⟨v,u⟩ρ​=∫ab​v∗(x)u(x)ρ(x)dx
(41)

  • Orthogonality condition of the eigenfunctions corresponding to different eigenvalues:

∫abv∗(x)u(x)ρ(x) dx=0ifλu≠λv\int_a^b v^*(x) u(x)\rho(x) \, dx = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad \lambda_u \neq \lambda_v∫ab​v∗(x)u(x)ρ(x)dx=0ifλu​=λv​
(42)

  • The weight may arise from coordinates, material coefficients, or the integrating factor used to put an equation into self-adjoint form.

Interval and boundary conditions¶

  • A set of conditions that ensures the SL operator LLL is Hermitian over the range [a,b] is the vanishing of the boundary term:

[v∗(x)p(x)dudx−p(x)dv∗(x)dxu(x)]ab=0\left[ v^*(x) p(x) \frac{du}{dx} - p(x) \frac{d v^*(x)}{dx} u(x) \right]_a^b = 0[v∗(x)p(x)dxdu​−p(x)dxdv∗(x)​u(x)]ab​=0
(43)

  • If ppp vanishes or an endpoint is infinite, the problem may be singular. Vanishing ppp does not by itself guarantee self-adjointness for arbitrary functions; endpoint behavior and, when required, boundary conditions must still be analyzed.

  • Additionally, the weight function should satisfy the following conditions:

    • For a regular problem, ρ(x)\rho(x)ρ(x) is real and positive on the interval.

    • ρ(x)\rho(x)ρ(x) must not change sign in the interval.

Special functions¶

  • In many physical and engineering problems, second-order linear differential equations with variable coefficients arise. These equations often have solutions that cannot be expressed in terms of elementary functions but are instead defined as special functions. We will briefly consider here Legendre, Bessel, Hermite, and Laguerre functions.

Legendre’s Equation and Legendre Polynomials¶

  • Legendre’s differential equation is:

(1−x2)d2ydx2−2xdydx+n(n+1)y=0(1 - x^2) \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} - 2 x \frac{dy}{dx} + n(n + 1) y = 0(1−x2)dx2d2y​−2xdxdy​+n(n+1)y=0
(44)

where nnn is a non-negative integer.

  • The solutions to this equation are the Legendre polynomials Pn(x)P_n(x)Pn​(x), defined on the interval −1≤x≤1-1 \leq x \leq 1−1≤x≤1.

  • These polynomials are orthogonal with respect to the weight function w(x)=1w(x) = 1w(x)=1.

  • Properties:

    • Pn(x)P_n(x)Pn​(x) is a polynomial of degree nnn.

    • Orthogonality:

∫−11Pn(x)Pm(x) dx=0forn≠m\int_{-1}^{1} P_n(x) P_m(x) \, dx = 0 \quad \text{for} \quad n \neq m∫−11​Pn​(x)Pm​(x)dx=0forn=m
(45)

Bessel’s Equation and Bessel Functions¶

  • Bessel’s differential equation is:

x2d2ydx2+xdydx+(x2−ν2)y=0x^2 \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} + x \frac{dy}{dx} + (x^2 - \nu^2) y = 0x2dx2d2y​+xdxdy​+(x2−ν2)y=0
(46)

where ν\nuν is the order of the Bessel function.

  • The solutions are:

    • Bessel functions of the first kind, Jν(x)J_\nu(x)Jν​(x).

    • Bessel functions of the second kind, Yν(x)Y_\nu(x)Yν​(x).

  • Bessel functions appear in problems with cylindrical symmetry, e.g., heat conduction in a cylindrical rod or vibrations of a circular membrane.

  • Properties:

    • Series representation for Jν(x)J_\nu(x)Jν​(x):

Jν(x)=∑k=0∞(−1)kk! Γ(k+ν+1)(x2)2k+νJ_\nu(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^k}{k! \, \Gamma(k + \nu + 1)} \left( \frac{x}{2} \right)^{2k + \nu}Jν​(x)=k=0∑∞​k!Γ(k+ν+1)(−1)k​(2x​)2k+ν
(47)

  • Orthogonality over specific intervals with weight w(x)=xw(x) = xw(x)=x:

∫01Jν(αnx)Jν(αmx)x dx=0(n≠m),\int_0^1 J_\nu(\alpha_n x)J_\nu(\alpha_m x)x\,dx=0 \quad(n\ne m),∫01​Jν​(αn​x)Jν​(αm​x)xdx=0(n=m),
(48)

when αn\alpha_nαn​ and αm\alpha_mαm​ are distinct positive zeros of JνJ_\nuJν​.

Hermite’s Equation and Hermite Polynomials¶

  • Hermite’s differential equation is:

d2ydx2−2xdydx+2ny=0\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} - 2 x \frac{dy}{dx} + 2 n y = 0dx2d2y​−2xdxdy​+2ny=0
(49)

where nnn is a non-negative integer.

  • The solutions are the Hermite polynomials Hn(x)H_n(x)Hn​(x).

  • Properties:

    • Hn(x)H_n(x)Hn​(x) is a polynomial of degree nnn.

    • Orthogonality with weight w(x)=e−x2w(x) = e^{-x^2}w(x)=e−x2:

∫−∞∞Hn(x)Hm(x)e−x2dx=0forn≠m\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} H_n(x) H_m(x) e^{-x^2} dx = 0 \quad \text{for} \quad n \neq m∫−∞∞​Hn​(x)Hm​(x)e−x2dx=0forn=m
(50)

Laguerre’s Equation and Laguerre Polynomials¶

  • Laguerre’s differential equation is:

xd2ydx2+(1−x)dydx+ny=0x \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} + (1 - x) \frac{dy}{dx} + n y = 0xdx2d2y​+(1−x)dxdy​+ny=0
(51)

with nnn being a non-negative integer.

  • The solutions are the Laguerre polynomials Ln(x)L_n(x)Ln​(x), defined for x≥0x \geq 0x≥0.

  • Properties:

    • Ln(x)L_n(x)Ln​(x) is a polynomial of degree nnn.

    • Orthogonality with weight w(x)=e−xw(x) = e^{-x}w(x)=e−x:

∫0∞Ln(x)Lm(x)e−xdx=0forn≠m\int_0^\infty L_n(x) L_m(x) e^{-x} dx = 0 \quad \text{for} \quad n \neq m∫0∞​Ln​(x)Lm​(x)e−xdx=0forn=m
(52)

Motivation {#motivation .unnumbered}¶

The time-independent Schrödinger equation for a particle of mass mmm in a one-dimensional potential V(x)V(x)V(x) is

−ℏ22m y′′(x)+V(x)y(x)=E y(x).-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\, y''(x) + V(x) y(x) = E\, y(x).−2mℏ2​y′′(x)+V(x)y(x)=Ey(x).
(53)

This can be written in Sturm--Liouville (SL) form and analyzed using spectral theory. This project explores how modifying the potential affects bound-state eigenvalues and eigenfunctions.

Tasks {#tasks-1 .unnumbered}¶

  1. Rewrite the Schrödinger equation in Sturm--Liouville form

−(p(x)y′)′+q(x)y=λw(x)y,-(p(x) y')' + q(x) y = \lambda w(x) y,−(p(x)y′)′+q(x)y=λw(x)y,
(54)

and identify p(x)p(x)p(x), q(x)q(x)q(x), w(x)w(x)w(x), and λ\lambdaλ.

  1. Choose a potential well, for example:

V(x)={0,∣x∣<1,V0,∣x∣≥1,orV(x)=x4−2x2.V(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & |x| < 1,\\ V_0, & |x| \ge 1, \end{cases} \quad \text{or}\quad V(x) = x^4 - 2x^2.V(x)={0,V0​,​∣x∣<1,∣x∣≥1,​orV(x)=x4−2x2.
(55)

Describe qualitatively the expected number of bound states.

  1. Solve the eigenvalue problem numerically (shooting method or finite differences) to approximate the first several eigenvalues EnE_nEn​.

  2. Plot the corresponding eigenfunctions yn(x)y_n(x)yn​(x).

  3. Verify orthogonality of eigenfunctions under the appropriate weight

∫abw(x) yn(x)ym(x) dx=0,n≠m.\int_{a}^{b} w(x)\, y_n(x) y_m(x)\, dx = 0, \qquad n \ne m.∫ab​w(x)yn​(x)ym​(x)dx=0,n=m.
(56)

  1. Discuss how the shape of V(x)V(x)V(x) influences the spacing of eigenvalues.

Hints {#hints-1 .unnumbered}¶

  • In SL form, w(x)=1w(x)=1w(x)=1 for the Schrödinger equation.

  • For numerical work, impose y(a)=0y(a)=0y(a)=0 and y(b)=0y(b)=0y(b)=0 for sufficiently large ±a\pm a±a.

  • The shooting method converts the problem into root-finding for the eigenvalue EEE.

  • Use symmetry: for even potentials, eigenfunctions are even or odd.

Motivation {#motivation-1 .unnumbered}¶

The classical eigenvalue problem

y′′(x)+λy(x)=0,x∈(0,L),y''(x) + \lambda y(x) = 0,\qquad x\in(0,L),y′′(x)+λy(x)=0,x∈(0,L),
(57)

arises in vibration, heat conduction, and quantum mechanics. Different boundary conditions produce different eigenvalue spectra, even though the differential equation is the same.

Tasks {#tasks-2 .unnumbered}¶

  1. Solve the problem under the following boundary conditions:

    • Dirichlet--Dirichlet: y(0)=0y(0)=0y(0)=0, y(L)=0y(L)=0y(L)=0.

    • Neumann--Neumann: y′(0)=0y'(0)=0y′(0)=0, y′(L)=0y'(L)=0y′(L)=0.

    • Mixed: y(0)=0y(0)=0y(0)=0, y′(L)=0y'(L)=0y′(L)=0.

    • Robin: y′(0)+hy(0)=0y'(0)+hy(0)=0y′(0)+hy(0)=0, y′(L)+hy(L)=0y'(L)+hy(L)=0y′(L)+hy(L)=0.

    For each case, derive the eigenvalue equation determining λ\lambdaλ.

  2. Determine how the eigenvalues depend on the type of boundary condition.

  3. Plot the first three eigenfunctions for each case.

  4. Discuss how the choice of boundary condition changes:

    • the fundamental frequency,

    • spacing between eigenvalues,

    • orthogonality relations,

    • completeness of eigenfunctions.

Hints {#hints-2 .unnumbered}¶

  • For Robin conditions, the eigenvalue equation involves tangent or cotangent functions.

  • The Neumann problem has λ0=0\lambda_0 = 0λ0​=0; interpret the physical meaning of the constant solution.

  • Use normalized eigenfunctions for clean comparisons.

  • Symmetry of boundary conditions often gives symmetric eigenfunctions.

Motivation {#motivation-2 .unnumbered}¶

Many SL problems cannot be solved analytically. This project compares numerical methods for computing eigenvalues of

−(p(x)y′)′+q(x)y=λw(x)y,x∈(a,b).-(p(x) y')' + q(x) y = \lambda w(x) y, \qquad x\in(a,b).−(p(x)y′)′+q(x)y=λw(x)y,x∈(a,b).
(58)

Tasks {#tasks-3 .unnumbered}¶

  1. Select a nontrivial SL operator, e.g.

p(x)=1+x,q(x)=sin⁡x,w(x)=1.p(x)=1+x,\quad q(x)=\sin x,\quad w(x)=1.p(x)=1+x,q(x)=sinx,w(x)=1.
(59)

  1. Implement the following three numerical approaches:

    1. Shooting method with root-finding.

    2. Finite-difference discretization leading to a matrix eigenvalue problem.

    3. Rayleigh--Ritz or Galerkin method using trial basis functions.

  2. Compute the first 3--5 eigenvalues for your chosen operator.

  3. Compare:

    • accuracy,

    • computational cost,

    • stability,

    • implementation difficulty.

  4. Plot the eigenfunctions for each method and compare visually.

  5. Discuss which method is most suitable for general SL problems.

Hints {#hints-3 .unnumbered}¶

  • To avoid instability in the shooting method, start integration from a regular endpoint.

  • The finite-difference method leads to a tridiagonal matrix that can be diagonalized efficiently.

  • In Galerkin, use orthogonal basis functions (e.g. sines or Legendre polynomials) to improve convergence.

  • Check eigenvalue convergence by refining your discretization.
